planting.note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Nesbitt is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) muscadine and does not require a separate pollinator vine. Train on a sturdy trellis or pergola; ripens mid-season, typically late August in the Gulf South.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; prune heavily each winter to renew fruiting wood on a two-wire trellis or arbor. Nesbitt is a University of Georgia-released muscadine selected for its combination of very large, deep purple-black fruit, vigorous productive vines, and reliable self-fertility, making it a popular home-garden choice that needs no separate pollinator vine. The fruit has a thin, tender skin for a muscadine, sweet juicy flesh, and good flavor for fresh eating, with fruit size among the largest of the widely grown self-fertile varieties. The vigorous vine bears heavily once established and holds its crop well, tolerating the humid, disease-prone conditions of Gulf South summers better than bunch grapes. A dependable, high-yielding choice for a home muscadine arbor in zone 7–9.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Muscadine Grape Varieties for Home Gardens

planting.note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Tara is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) bronze muscadine and does not require a separate pollinator vine. Train on a sturdy trellis or pergola; ripens early-to-mid season.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; train onto a sturdy trellis and prune heavily each winter to renew fruiting wood. Tara is a University of Georgia-released bronze muscadine grown for its consistently high fruit quality — large, uniform, golden-bronze berries with sweet, richly flavored flesh and a relatively tender skin — combined with a self-fertile, productive vine that bears reliably without a separate pollinator variety. It ripens earlier in the season than many bronze muscadines, extending the harvest window when planted alongside later-ripening varieties, and the fruit holds well on the vine without excessive cracking or splitting in humid weather. Widely recommended for both fresh eating and home winemaking, Tara is a strong choice for a Gulf South home muscadine planting, zone 7–9.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Muscadine Grape Varieties for Home Gardens

planting.note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Sugargate is self-fertile (perfect-flowered) and does not require a separate pollinator vine, though it is a lighter producer than some varieties and benefits from attentive pruning and fertility to maximize yield.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile, slightly acidic to neutral soil; train onto a sturdy trellis and prune to a well-spaced fruiting framework each winter. Sugargate is a University of Georgia-released black muscadine grown almost entirely for exceptional fresh-eating quality — its large, tender-skinned fruit carries the highest sugar content and richest, sweetest flavor of any widely planted muscadine cultivar, making it a favorite among home growers and muscadine enthusiasts who prioritize taste over yield. The vine is somewhat less vigorous and productive than heavier-bearing varieties like Nesbitt or Supreme, so it is often planted as a specialty dessert selection alongside a more prolific cultivar rather than as the sole vine in a planting. Give it full sun, good drainage, and attentive care to get the best from its outstanding flavor, zone 7–9.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Muscadine Grape Varieties for Home Gardens

planting.note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Southern Home is self-fertile and does not require a separate pollinator vine; train onto an arbor or pergola where its ornamental, deeply lobed foliage can be shown off along with its fruit.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; train onto a sturdy arbor or pergola, where the vine doubles as an ornamental landscape feature. Southern Home is a distinctive interspecific hybrid between muscadine grape (Vitis rotundifolia) and traditional bunch grape (Vitis vinifera), bred at the University of Georgia specifically for its uniquely ornamental, deeply lobed, almost oak-leaf-shaped foliage that sets it visually apart from the simple rounded leaves of standard muscadine varieties, making it a popular dual-purpose choice for a decorative fruiting arbor. The self-fertile vine produces medium-sized, black, muscadine-flavored fruit in loose bunches more reminiscent of a traditional grape cluster than the typical loose, few-berried muscadine set, and it carries good resistance to Pierce's disease inherited from its muscadine parentage — a critical advantage over standard bunch grapes in the humid Gulf South and Southeast, where Pierce's disease kills most vinifera and many hybrid grapes outright. An excellent choice for gardeners who want both fruit and ornamental landscape value from the same vine, zone 6–9.
sources: University of Georgia Extension — Muscadine Grape Varieties for Home Gardens
North Carolina State University Extension — Muscadine Grape Cultivar Guide

planting.note: Plant dormant cuttings or container-grown vines in spring; in zone 9 plant February–April. Alachua is a perfect-flowered (self-fertile) black muscadine bred by the University of Florida for Deep South and Florida growing conditions, and does not require a separate pollinator vine.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; train onto a sturdy trellis or arbor and prune heavily each winter to maintain productive fruiting wood. Alachua is a University of Florida-released black muscadine bred and selected specifically for the low-chill, high-heat, high-humidity conditions of Florida and the Deep South, where it produces large, high-quality fruit reliably even in areas too warm for many Georgia- and Carolina-bred muscadine cultivars. The self-fertile vine is vigorous and productive, bearing medium-to-large black fruit with good sweetness and flavor well suited to both fresh eating and processing. Its Florida-focused breeding makes it a particularly strong choice for muscadine growers in the warmest parts of the Gulf South, zone 7–10.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Muscadine Grape Cultivars for Florida
